displayQuote: Half of the Town Councilors Are Not Fools

meta.title: Who really said "Half of the Town Councilors Are Not Fools"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Disraeli. The earliest version is a July 1927 newspaper story about a Swedish town councillor; the Disraeli version appears in 1958, 77 years after his death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Half of the Town Councilors Are Not Fools'?
meta.ogDescription: A 1927 Swedish newspaper joke, attached to Disraeli in 1958. Hansard has no record of it.

answer.label: Not Disraeli — a Swedish newspaper story from 1927
answer.authorName: Unknown — popularly credited to Benjamin Disraeli
answer.authorDates: Anonymous newspaper anecdote · first printed July 1927 · attached to Disraeli by 1958
answer.sourceLine: The dates settle it. Disraeli died in 1881; the earliest telling of this joke that Quote Investigator could find was printed in July 1927, in a story about a municipal councillor in an unnamed town near Uppsala, Sweden, who was made to apologise and posted bills reading ‘I said that half of the town councilors are fools. I now declare that half of the town councilors are not fools.’ It reached Disraeli’s name in 1958, in a reference book on Parliament. QI searched the Hansard record and did not find the exchange.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: An unnamed town near Uppsala, Sweden

source.excerpt: A municipal councilor … remarked that certainly half of his colleagues were fools. An apology was demanded. He promised to make reparation and caused bills with the following correction to be posted on boardings in the town: “I said that half of the town councilors are fools. I now declare that half of the town councilors are not fools.”
trail: Quote Investigator’s earliest instance is the July 1927 Swedish story, and the earliest evidence it found linking the tale to Disraeli is An Encyclopaedia of Parliament by Norman Wilding and Philip Laundy, 1958: quoteinvestigator.com ↗.
QI states that it searched the Hansard database of parliamentary transcripts and has not found evidence of the retraction, and that it also searched for variants using ‘fools’, ‘knaves’ and ‘idiots’.

The joke was never fixed to one target. QI traces it to aldermen in The Sydney Mail in 1930, to an unnamed town in The Montreal Gazette in 1933, to a South African parliament in 1963 and to the Israeli Knesset in 1968.
Neither the sourced nor the misattributed section of Wikiquote’s Disraeli page carries this line in any form: en.wikiquote.org ↗.
source.excerptNote: Quote Investigator reports the same story in the Syracuse Herald and The Milwaukee Journal within the same month. No speaker is named in any of them.

author.name: Benjamin Disraeli
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Disraeli
author.metaLine: 1804–1881 · British Prime Minister, novelist and parliamentary wit
author.bio: Benjamin Disraeli was twice Prime Minister and, by common consent, the most quotable speaker of the Victorian Commons — which has made him one of the standing magnets for unattributed political wit. A great deal of what circulates under his name was said later, by someone else, or by nobody in particular. His Wikiquote page carries a long misattributed section for exactly this reason, and it does not include this line.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A joke with no author and a long list of borrowed ones. Disraeli is simply the most quotable name it has been pinned to.

items.why: He died in 1881; the story first appears in 1927 and reaches his name in 1958. Quote Investigator searched Hansard and found nothing: Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: An unnamed councillor near Uppsala, Sweden
items.why: The July 1927 newspaper story that Quote Investigator identifies as the earliest instance names nobody: Quote Investigator ↗.

Skinner did make a related retraction joke in the Commons in 1981 — offering to agree that a member ‘was there the other half’ — but it is a different line, and Quote Investigator transcribes it from the Hansard record: Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous Swedish newspaper anecdote from 1927, retold about aldermen, cabinets and parliaments for a century, and given to Disraeli in 1958: Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke turns on a rule of parliamentary manners: you may be forced to withdraw an insult, but nobody can stop you withdrawing it in a form that insults again. That is why it keeps being relocated to whichever legislature the teller finds funniest.
It attaches to Disraeli because he genuinely was the great parliamentary wit of the Victorian Commons — which makes the story plausible enough that few people check it.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator traces the anecdote through The Sydney Mail (1930, aldermen and a newspaper editor), The Montreal Gazette (1933), Casey Motsisi in DRUM magazine (reprinted 1963) and a 1968 memoir relocating it to the Israeli parliament.
The 1958 attribution comes from An Encyclopaedia of Parliament, which called the occasion famous — a reference book asserting fame is often the moment an anecdote becomes a fact.
